From the body a long dark/black cylindrical infrared telescope tube with a sunshade extends at an angle, roughly as long as the body is tall, with a ribbed outer surface. Two deployable solar wings stick out on opposite sides; each wing is a stepped cross shape: an inner panel of dark blue cells (about 3 columns by 2 rows) plus an outer panel offset higher, giving each wing a staircase silhouette; cells dark blue in light grid frames. A small antenna on a thin angled boom with a forked tip projects from the lower side of the body; small sensor boxes and rod antennas around the top. Wing span several times the body width.

draw-tselina-r.description: Soviet Yuzhnoye-built signals-intelligence satellite (about 1.75-2 t), same layout as Tselina-D and the civilian Sich/Okean. Body is a tall vertical pressurised cylinder, light grey-green with white bands, its lower part slightly wider, topped by a short tapering cone and a small open-frame cage of struts. From the top a long thin gravity-gradient boom rises straight up, about as long as the body or longer, ending in a small ball/end mass. Two deployable solar panels attach to the middle of the cylinder on opposite sides, angled outward and upward like ears; each is a roughly square panel of dark blue cells in a grid. Around the base ring several long, flat, blade-shaped light grey/white antenna panels radiate horizontally outward like the spokes of a flat star, each as long as the body is wide, with thin wire/whip antennas with small forked (red-tipped in the Yuzhnoye drawing) ends hanging between them. Overall silhouette: a vertical rocket-like cylinder standing on a flat star of blades with two solar ears and a tall mast.

draw-zaliv-tsiklon.description: Soviet first-generation navigation satellite (NPO PM / Reshetnev, KAUR-1 drum bus, about 800 kg). Body is an upright drum (cylinder) about 2 m in diameter and 3 m long (roughly 1.5 times as long as wide). The whole curved side is covered with dark blue-black body-mounted solar cells laid out as a grid of rectangular panels separated by thin silver seams; no large deployable solar wings on the original Tsiklon. One end has a lighter silver/white ring and end plate with a short conical or boxy fitting in the centre; from this end a single very thin straight gravity-gradient boom extends far out, many times the drum length, with a tiny end mass at its tip. A few thin rod/whip antennas stick out at angles from the opposite end of the drum. Reference pictures: Reshetnev drawing of the original Tsyklon (blue cell-covered drum, long thin boom) and Reshetnev assembly photo of the closely related Parus on the same bus (black cell-covered drum with a small open lattice mast and antenna cluster on top). The VDNKh display copy of Tsyklon/Parus additionally shows two small square lattice panels near the top end; omit them unless drawing the later Parus version.

refs: https://www.eoportal.org/satellite-missions/transit (Figure 6: Artist's view of the Nova spacecraft, JHU/APL)
draw-nova.description: US Navy Transit navigation satellite of the improved NOVA series (RCA-built from the JHU/APL TIP design, about 170 kg). Central body is a short cylindrical/octagonal drum, silver-grey, only about as wide as it is tall (well under 1 m). Four long, narrow rectangular deployable solar paddles stick straight out from the body in a flat plus/cross shape, at 90 degrees to each other; each paddle is a slender blade several times the body diameter long, with blue cells on a white frame, attached to the body by a short thin strut. From the top of the body a long boom rises at a slant: a cylindrical silver DISCOS drag-compensation module sits just above the body, then a long open lattice (triangular-truss) boom about 6 m long, ending in a rounded copper/orange-coloured end mass shaped like a short barrel with domed ends. Underside (Earth-facing) carries short antenna stubs. Silhouette: a flat four-bladed cross with a tall thin lattice mast and a copper knob on top. Based on the single JHU/APL artist's view of Nova.

draw-argos.description: Large USAF Space Test Program experiment satellite (Boeing/Rockwell, 2,720 kg). Body is a big boxy rectangular bus, roughly cube-like but a little longer than wide, its faces pale silver-grey / light blue-grey with a cluttered surface of many instrument boxes bolted on (nine experiments). One end face carries a gold/amber foil-wrapped section. On the side facing forward there is a large square instrument aperture with a dark grid-like face (the USA X-ray instrument), plus small cylindrical telescopes and boxes (GIMI, HIRAAS, EUVIP) on the Earth-facing side and a small round radio beacon antenna (CERTO) and stubs on top. A short boom with a small thruster head (ESEX arcjet) projects from one face. Two deployable solar wings attach on opposite sides of the body via short yokes; each wing is three large square-ish panels in a row, together making a total span roughly six to seven times the body width; cells are deep blue in a fine grid with thin white gaps between panels. Wings are flat and in-line with each other, forming a long straight bar through the body.

draw-forte.description: Los Alamos/Sandia lightning and radio-transient satellite (210 kg). Body is an eight-sided (octagonal) column about 2.1 m tall and roughly 1 m across, built as three stacked octagonal cages: the upper cage tapers inward toward a smaller flat octagonal top deck, giving a bullet/tapered-lantern shape. All side facets are covered with body-mounted solar panels: dark blue cells in a regular grid with white/silver framing (24 solar panels, no deployable wings). The top deck is plain white/silver; a small round sensor port sits on one side facet. From the bottom (nadir) end a long, thin, open lattice mast about 11 m long extends straight down (many times the body length), orange/copper-coloured, threaded through a row of grey ring-shaped spacers evenly spaced along it. Along the mast stick out pairs of thin straight orange antenna rods in two perpendicular planes, longest near the body (up to about 5 m tip-to-tip) and shortening toward the far end: a log-periodic turnstile antenna that looks like a giant tapering fishbone/TV aerial.

draw-kitsat-3.description: Korean remote-sensing microsatellite (110 kg), a rectangular box 49.5 x 60.4 x 85.2 cm, taller than wide. Body walls are covered in shiny gold/copper-coloured foil and aluminium honeycomb panels. Four flat rectangular solar panels, each the full height of a side, are hinged along the vertical body edges and swing open like doors/wings (two shown open on either side in the deployed illustration); panels carry dark blue-black solar cells in vertical strips with silver frame edges. On one broad face: a short dark-green/black cylindrical camera tube (MEIS, 10 cm aperture) sticking straight out, a round silver disc (electron temperature probe), and two small flat square patch antennas (S-band and X-band) near the bottom. On the top deck: two small cylindrical star-sensor tubes, a small box with a funnel (particle telescope), a sun sensor and an Earth-horizon sensor box. A short magnetometer rod sits on one panel tip. Base sits on a round separation ring.

draw-kompsat-1.description: Korean Earth-observation satellite (TRW-heritage bus, 470 kg). Body is a hexagonal prism 1.33 m across and 2.33 m long, lying lengthwise; its long flat side facets carry dark blue/violet body-mounted solar cells framed by bright gold foil, and the end caps and edges are gold/amber foil. At the Earth-facing end the body narrows into a gold-foiled instrument section with a square box carrying the round lens of the EOC camera and, below it, the OSMI ocean scanner box. Two deployable solar wings stick out on opposite sides near the middle of the body, each on a short boom; each wing is a long narrow strip of about four to five rectangular panels in a row with dark blue cells and thin white gaps between panels, total span about four times the body length. A thin rod with a small dish-shaped antenna hangs below the instrument end, and small sensors/booms project from the body. Colour scheme: gold foil plus deep blue cells.

draw-viking-se.description: Sweden's first satellite (SAAB/Boeing, 520 kg with motor). Shape is a flat, wide octagonal disc 1.9 m across and only 0.5 m thick (pancake proportions, nearly four times wider than tall). In the flight photos the side walls are wrapped in crinkled silver thermal blanket with large gold-foil panels on the facets; the top face is covered in crinkled silver foil inside a prominent riveted metal ring (a copy of the Ariane payload-adapter ring, which SPOT 1 sat on), with small white and boxy instruments and a pair of fat foil-wrapped cylindrical camera tubes (auroral UV imager) poking out of one edge. Under the disc, at the centre, is the bell-shaped nozzle of a Star 26C rocket motor. Spin-stabilised; once in orbit four very thin wire antennas 40 m long are spooled out radially from the rim (like the spokes of a huge wheel, far longer than the body), two stiff 4 m rods extend axially up and down from the centre, each wire/rod ending in a small sensor ball, and two short radial booms carry magnetometer heads. Solar cells are not clearly visible in the available photos; draw the body as described (silver/gold foil disc) rather than inventing wing panels.

draw-iss-b-ume.description: Japanese ionosphere-sounding satellite (NASDA, 141 kg, spin-stabilised). Body is a short cylinder (many-sided drum) about 94 cm in diameter and 82 cm tall, slightly wider than tall. The whole curved side is covered by body-mounted solar cells arranged as an irregular patchwork of small dark grey-blue rectangular panels with silver gaps, giving a shiny mosaic look; top and bottom edges have a thin silver rim. No deployable wings. Beneath the drum (as photographed on its launch adapter) is a narrower silver equipment base. Ionosonde sounding antennas (long wire dipoles) were deployed in orbit but are not shown in the reference photo; if drawn, show them as very thin straight wires extending from the rim. Based on one JAXA pre-launch photo of the Ume series.

draw-mos-1.description: Japan's first Earth-observation satellite type (NEC/NASDA, 740 kg); MOS-1b is identical to MOS-1. Body is a rectangular box about 1.3 x 1.5 x 2.4 m covered almost entirely in bright gold/orange foil, with a busy surface of smaller protruding boxes, square sensor windows and two round white/silver radiometer dish-faces (the MSR microwave radiometer) on the Earth-facing side. A single deployable solar paddle (one wing only) extends from one side of the box on a short boom: a long, narrow, flat rectangular wing many times the body length, with dark blue cells, angled away from the body. Asymmetric silhouette: gold box at one end, single long blue wing trailing off to the other side.

draw-magion-5.description: Czech magnetospheric subsatellite of the Interball-2 project (Institute of Atmospheric Physics, Prague, 68.5 kg, spin-stabilised with spin axis toward the Sun); Magion 4 and 5 are the same design. Body is a squat octagonal (eight-sided) prism less than 1 m across, its side facets covered with small dark blue solar cell panels in white frames and the end face a silver/white plate with small red-capped sensors, connectors and a central round instrument. From the body radiate eight deployable solar paddles in a star/cross pattern (four long and four shorter, alternating), each a narrow rectangular strip of two or three dark-blue cell panels in white aluminium frames, the long ones ending in a dark-grey plain tip panel with a small gold-coloured disc sensor. Many thin black whip antennas and wire booms stick out between the paddles, two of them ending in small black spheres (probes), and a small white dish-shaped sensor sits on a short side boom. Solar power is 8 groups of small 196 mm square cell panels (SB1-8). Red protective tags/caps dot the structure in the lab photo (omit in flight). Note: the different-looking Magion museum model on Wikimedia Commons is an earlier Magion type, not this design. Overall: a spiky eight-armed star with a cell-covered octagonal hub.

draw-hilat.description: USAF/DNA ionospheric research satellite built by JHU/APL from the refurbished Navy Transit 'Oscar 16' navigation satellite. Small, compact central body (well under 1 m across), a short multi-sided drum with stacked equipment decks, light grey/white. Four long, narrow, flat solar panels, each 167.6 cm long by 25.4 cm wide, stick straight out from the middle of the body at right angles to each other in a flat cross/windmill shape, so the span is several times the body size; panels have dark blue-black cells with lighter frame edges. Short whip/dipole antennas stick out at the tips of two opposing panels, and a small magnetometer sensor sits at the tip of another. From the top of the body a very long thin gravity-gradient boom (the 85-foot / about 26 m Transit boom) rises straight up, many times the panel length, ending in a small knob-shaped end mass. On the bottom (Earth-facing) side: small instrument boxes (drift meter, particle spectrometer), a short beacon antenna, and the Auroral Ionospheric Mapper scanner. Silhouette: a flat four-armed cross with a hair-thin mast.

draw-polar-bear.description: USAF/DNA auroral research satellite built by JHU/APL from the 1963 Transit 'Oscar 17' navigation satellite that had hung in the Smithsonian; a museum piece flown to space. The original Oscar body is a small white hexagonal drum; APL stacked new sections on it: a 'pedestal' with box-shaped electronics on top, and below it a 'penthouse' and a wide, flat, round experiment deck (a disc noticeably wider than the body) on the Earth-facing end, from which a stubby cylindrical beacon antenna and the boxy AIRS auroral imager scanner project downward. Four long, narrow, flat solar panels (about 1.7 m / 5.5 ft long each, quite slender) radiate from the body at right angles in a flat cross, like the sails of a windmill; dark blue-black cells, light edges. Small forked dipole antennas sit at the tips of two opposite panels and a triaxial magnetometer sensor at the tip of another. A very thin Bi-STEM gravity-gradient boom rises straight up from the top, ending in a small round eddy-current damper ball. Body light grey/white with Teflon-white surfaces.

draw-wideband-p76-5.description: USAF Space Test Program radio-propagation satellite built by JHU/APL on the Navy Transit 'Oscar 15' navigation satellite (73 kg), carrying only a multi-frequency radio beacon. No picture of Wideband itself was found; draw it as the standard Transit Oscar: a small, short octagonal/cylindrical drum body (roughly 0.5 m across), silver-grey/white with gold detailing, with four long narrow flat solar paddles sticking straight out at right angles in a flat cross (each paddle several times the body diameter, dark blue cells with white frames), a very long hair-thin gravity-gradient boom rising from the top ending in a small dark end mass, and short antenna stubs on the Earth-facing underside. Same family look as HILAT and Polar BEAR, but without their added instrument decks.

draw-swas.description: NASA Small Explorer radio telescope (GSFC bus, Ball telescope, 288 kg), about 1.63 m tall and 1.02 m across. Body is an upright column: the lower spacecraft bus is a squat, slightly tapered drum wrapped in dark/black and gold foil with small square radiator patches; above it the instrument section is a cluster of shiny silver cylinders (receiver and electronics housings) with orange/gold foil between them, all capped at the top by a flat round/oval dark sun-shade lid over the telescope opening (the telescope is a 55 x 71 cm elliptical off-axis Cassegrain dish inside). A thin gold-foiled strut and small instruments run up one side. Two deployable solar wings stick out on opposite sides from the middle of the body; each wing is two large flat rectangular panels hinged together end to end, the wing slightly bent at the hinge, shown pale silver-grey/white in the NASA artwork with thin dark frame lines; total span roughly four times the body width.

draw-toms-ep.description: NASA ozone-mapping satellite built by TRW (T100/Eagle bus, about 295 kg). Body is a squat multi-sided (hexagonal) prism, silver-grey with a ribbed/panelled look, about as tall as wide, with the TOMS instrument (a small box with a scanning window) on the Earth-facing end. Two flat deployable solar wings stick out on opposite sides from the upper body on short booms; each wing is mid/light blue and roughly rectangular but with a distinctive scalloped outer end made of three rounded lobes (like a rounded three-fingered paddle), with small dark rectangular cut-outs/fittings. Wings are wider than the body is tall and together span about three to four body widths. Based only on low-resolution NASA animation frames, so fine details are uncertain.

draw-topex-poseidon.description: NASA/CNES ocean-altimetry satellite (Fairchild Multimission Modular Spacecraft bus, 2,400 kg). Body is a long, boxy assembly about 5.5 m long, 6.6 m tall and 2.8 m deep, made of two parts: a satellite bus module (a triangular-section MMS frame carrying three square-faced subsystem boxes: attitude control, power and propulsion, faced in light grey/white with louvre radiators) and a larger rectangular instrument module wrapped in bright gold/amber foil with some pale blue-grey panels. On the Earth-facing underside: a large round 1.5 m radar-altimeter dish pointing straight down, ringed by laser retroreflector cubes, plus a small downward rod (DORIS antenna) at one corner. On one end: a round microwave-radiometer reflector. From the top: a 1.2 m white high-gain dish on a short mast, and a very tall thin mast carrying a small flat disc GPS antenna. A single, very large, flat rectangular solar wing extends to one side on a boom: 8.9 m long by 3.3 m wide, four large panels in a row, dark blue/grey cells; the wing is longer than the body. Asymmetric silhouette: gold box with one huge flat panel.

draw-radarsat-1.description: Canadian radar Earth-observation satellite (Ball Aerospace bus, 3,200 kg). Central body is an upright rectangular box (bus module below, SAR payload module above) wrapped in crinkled gold/bronze foil with a few square blue radiator panels and small antennas on top. Its defining feature is a very long, flat, narrow SAR antenna running horizontally underneath and to both sides: 15 m long by 1.5 m wide, five panels end to end, also covered in crinkled gold foil, held to the body by a thin triangular strut frame. Above it, two deployable solar wings stick out on opposite sides on short angled struts (V-shaped attachments); each wing is five tall rectangular panels side by side with deep blue cells in a fine grid and thin silver edges. Silhouette: a gold box with two blue wings above and a long gold plank below, about the same total length as the wing span.

draw-spot-mk1.description: French Earth-observation satellite on the SPOT Mk.1 bus (Matra, about 1,800 kg), identical to SPOT 1 and 3. Body is a long rectangular box, roughly 2 x 2 m in section and about twice as long, entirely covered in crinkled bright gold foil, with square white/silver radiator windows set in rows on the sides and a small round white dish antenna on the underside. At the front end sit the two HRV cameras: two large gold-foiled instrument housings side by side, each ending in an angled box-shaped mirror head (the steerable viewing mirrors), giving the front a chunky twin-snouted look. A single deployable solar wing on a boom sticks out from the rear end on one side only, roughly perpendicular to the body: a long flat strip of square panels with deep blue cells and thin white gaps, about as long as or longer than the body. Asymmetric silhouette: gold box with one long blue wing. It has ONLY ONE solar wing, on one side; the other side has no wing at all.

draw-spot-4.description: French Earth-observation satellite on the larger SPOT Mk.2 bus (about 2,750 kg). Same family look as SPOT 1-3 but bigger: a long rectangular box covered in bright gold foil with darker rectangular radiator patches and square windows on the sides, and small antennas below. At the front, the two HRVIR cameras form a pair of large gold-foiled housings with angled mirror heads, and a smaller boxy VEGETATION wide-angle camera sits on top with a round lens. A single solar wing on a boom extends from the rear on one side: five large rectangular panels (25 m2 total, 8,640 silicon cells) with pale lavender-blue cells, drawn in the CNES artwork as a tall sheet of squares two panels wide. Asymmetric silhouette: gold box with one large flat wing.

draw-sunsat.description: South Africa's first satellite (Stellenbosch University students, 64 kg). Body is an upright rectangular box 45 x 45 x 62 cm (slightly taller than wide), built as stacked trays between a base and top plate. All four sides are covered edge to edge with body-mounted solar panels: very dark blue-black cells in a dense fine grid with thin copper/red edging and silver corner rails (no deployable wings). The top plate is silver/gold with sensors (horizon, sun and star sensors) and the boom canister; one side (the bottom/nadir face) has a round imager aperture, the camera being a 10 cm telescope tube. Several thin straight whip antennas stick out at angles from the edges of the box. From the top a thin gravity-gradient boom about 2.5-3 m long (several times the body height) extends straight out, ending in a squat round tip mass (about 4.4 kg) shaped like a short drum ringed with corner-cube laser reflectors (a hemispherical annulus of 8 retroreflectors).

draw-sstl-dga-elint.description: Two 50 kg French military signals-intelligence microsatellites on the Surrey Satellite Technology Microsat-70 platform (Cerise 1995, its successor Clementine 1999; the 1999 'CLEMENTINE' is this French satellite, not NASA's lunar probe). Body is a compact upright box roughly 0.5 m on a side (about as tall as wide in the SSTL photos); every side wall is a body-mounted solar panel of very dark navy-blue cells in a fine grid of thin gold/silver interconnect lines, framed with thin red/copper edging and silver corner rails. The top plate is plain silver aluminium with a large round flange plate in the centre carrying a short silver cylinder (the gravity-gradient boom canister), small boxes at the corners and thin straight rod antennas angled up from the corners. At the base, four flat rectangular deployable solar panels are hinged to the bottom edges and fold outward and downward like the petals of an opening flower (dark backs with red wiring and silver hinge bars visible). In orbit a thin gravity-gradient boom about 6 m long extends from the top (Cerise lost about 4.2 m of its boom to a debris collision in 1996, the first verified satellite collision).

refs: https://www.eoportal.org/satellite-missions/fasat-bravo (sister SSTL microsat launched on the same Zenit: 60 x 36 x 36 cm)
draw-tmsat-1.description: Thailand's first satellite, an SSTL-built microsatellite (55 kg) for Mahanakorn University. Body is a tall upright rectangular box roughly 36 x 36 cm in section and about 60 cm tall (the size of its SSTL sister FASat-Bravo, launched on the same rocket) (under shoulder height of a person). All four sides are body-mounted solar panels: very dark navy-black GaAs cells (2 x 4 cm each, 42 per panel string) in a dense grid with tiny gold contacts, each side split into an upper and lower panel by a thin red/maroon bar, framed by red-brown edging and clear/silver corner rails. On the top deck sit small red/pink anodised boxes with four short monopole whip antennas (thin silver/black rods) angled up from the corners, plus two fatter rods; the bottom has a round separation ring and more monopoles. A gravity-gradient boom with a small end weight extends from the top in orbit. No deployable wings. Carries small wide-angle and narrow-angle cameras looking out of the base.

draw-aureole-3.description: Soviet-French auroral research satellite (Interkosmos AUOS-type platform, about 1,030 kg). Central body is a pressurised cylinder 1.6 m in diameter and 2.7 m tall, silver/white metal. Its sun-facing end is a flat round end plate (silver-white, with the name 'OREOL-3' in Cyrillic in red/black letters on the photographed unit) studded around its rim with a ring of small round sensor ports. Around this end, eight deployable flat solar panels fan out radially like the petals of a sunflower or the blades of a windmill: each is a rectangular panel, longer than it is wide, slightly wider at its outer end, with a pale grey/silver surface divided by a grid of cell lines, attached by short struts so there is a gap between the panels and the drum. Between the panels stick out several thin sensor booms (six instrument booms in total), short rod antennas and a small white cylindrical sensor and dish. Silhouette from the end: a round hub with an eight-petalled ring of panels and spiky booms; from the side: a squat cylinder with a flared skirt of panels at one end. Gravity-gradient/magnetic stabilised.

draw-astrid-2.description: Swedish auroral-research microsatellite (Swedish Space Corporation, 29-30 kg), spin-stabilised and Sun-pointing, said to be 'about the size and weight of an overhead projector'. Body is a low square box 45 x 45 x 30 cm (wider than tall), silver/black with small instruments on its faces (a round MEDUSA particle analyser on one side, the PIA photometer on top). Six solar panels in total: two fixed on the top face and four deployable flat rectangular panels hinged to the top edges that swing out horizontally, all in one plane facing the spin axis (toward the Sun), giving a flat cross/plus shape about 1.7 x 1.1 m; cells dark. Two short (0.61 m) thin booms stick out from the tips of two opposite panels, each ending in a tiny 10 mm sphere (Langmuir probes), and four very long hair-thin wire booms with small probes extend radially in the spin plane. A hinged two-part rod boom hangs below the box carrying the magnetometer and a star camera at its end.

draw-cbers-1.description: China-Brazil Earth-resources satellite (CAST Phoenix-Eye 1 bus, 1,450 kg). Body is an upright rectangular box 1.8 x 2.0 x 2.2 m, wrapped almost entirely in bright yellow-gold foil, made of a lower service module and an upper payload module with a horizontal band between them. A single large deployable solar wing (one side only) sticks out from one upper side on a short angled yoke: 6.3 m long by 2.6 m wide, three tall rectangular panels side by side, deep blue cells with thin lighter panel gaps; the wing is much bigger than the body. On the Earth-facing bottom face: the CCD camera and infrared scanner apertures, a WFI wide-field camera, small thruster clusters, and several antennas, including a long straight downward rod (UHF/VHF) and short stubby S-band and UHF antennas at the lower corners; a small sun sensor and two short rod antennas on top. Silhouette: a gold box with one big blue rectangular sail.

draw-diamant-a.description: A spent solid-rocket upper stage drifting and slowly tumbling in orbit, no flame, no exhaust. A plain, slender cylinder about 2.0 m long overall and 0.66 m in diameter (roughly 3 to 1), made of filament-wound fibreglass with a smooth matte off-white ablative outer coating, faint helical winding texture, a few thin circumferential seams. Forward end: a short cylindrical skirt the same diameter, capped by a shallow domed cover with one small knob-like pressure fitting and a small stub radar-transponder antenna on the rim; on top sits an empty open payload adapter, a short squat white aluminium cone about 0.55 m across with four round lightening holes and a bolted ring, satellite gone. Aft end: a short open cylindrical skirt around the rounded rear dome, from which a single fixed nozzle protrudes about 0.4 m, an egg-cup-shaped flared bell nearly half the stage diameter at its mouth, dark charred brown-black composite. No fins, no fairing, no equipment bay, no spin rockets, no solar panels, no markings visible. The adapter cone sits on the FRONT END of the stage, in line with the cylinder’s axis, opposite the nozzle; nothing is attached to the side of the cylinder.

draw-diamant-bp4.description: A spent solid-rocket upper stage drifting and slowly tumbling in orbit, no flame, no exhaust. A stubby plain cylinder about 1.7 m long for the body and 0.80 m in diameter, about 2.1 m with the nozzle (roughly 2.6 to 1, noticeably fatter than a pencil), made of filament-wound fibreglass with a smooth matte off-white ablative outer coating, faint helical winding texture, thin circumferential seams. Forward end: a short cylindrical skirt the same diameter housing a narrow ring of electronics, closed by a shallow domed cover with a small stub antenna on its rim; on top an empty, short, open conical payload adapter ring about half the stage diameter, the small spherical satellite gone. Aft end: a short open cylindrical skirt around the rounded rear dome; a single fixed nozzle protrudes about 0.4 m, a flared egg-cup-shaped bell in dark charred brown-black composite. No fins, no fairing, no equipment bay, no spin rockets, no solar panels, no markings visible.

draw-strela-3.description: Small cylinder about 1.5 m tall and 1.0 m across, sides covered in body-mounted solar cells, one long gravity-gradient boom with a tip mass pointing away from Earth; no deployable solar wings. ~225 kg. Gonets-D1 is the civilian version and is described as similar, so the two can likely share a drawing. Earth's limb below has blue oceans and white clouds (not orange).

draw-tselina-2.description: Large (~3,200 kg) cylinder, an enlarged Tselina-D bus, about 4.5 m long and 1.4 m across, two deployable solar wings, plus a gravity-gradient boom; three-axis stabilised. Exact antenna layout not published. Earth's limb below has blue oceans and white clouds (not orange).

draw-strela-1m.description: Small octagonal-ish cylinder about 0.8 m across, all its sides covered in solar cells, short whip antennas, no solar wings. Earth's limb below has blue oceans and white clouds (not orange).

draw-sterkh.description: Small box about 1 m across with two flat rectangular solar panels on either side and one short antenna; from its Earth-facing end a very long, very thin gravity-gradient boom (many times longer than the body) runs straight down out of frame toward Earth, ending in a small tip weight. Earth's limb below has blue oceans and white clouds (not orange).

draw-myriade.description: ~60 cm cube, 100-200 kg; one or two deployable flat solar wings; payload-specific add-ons (DEMETER: long boom-mounted magnetometer/sensor arms; ELISA: small cubes with extra RF antennas, flown as a 4-ship cluster).

draw-cosmo-skymed.description: ~1,700 kg box-shaped bus (Thales Alenia PRIMA); long flat X-band SAR antenna panel (~5.7 x 1.4 m) along one side; two deployable solar wings; four identical craft.

draw-cubesat-3u.description: A tall narrow three-unit CubeSat: three 10 cm cubes stacked into one 10 x 10 x 34 cm bar with aluminium rails along its edges. Four long thin solar panels, each as long as the bar, are hinged at one end and fold out at an angle like petals. Thin tape-measure antennas stick out from the other end. Earth's limb below has blue oceans and white clouds (not orange).

draw-gomspace-16u.description: 16U CubeSat (~23 x 23 x 45 cm) by GomSpace; VHF antenna and ADS-B receiver antennas; solar panels (layout not confirmed).

draw-worldview-bcp5000.description: Tall ~3.6 m prism bus around a big telescope (aperture at one end), deployable solar arrays, CMG attitude control; ~2,500 kg.

draw-xss-10.description: 28 kg battery-powered micro-satellite with camera/star sensor and small thrusters; flew around the Delta II second stage.

draw-ims-1.description: Small (~60 cm) cube-ish box, ~80-90 kg, two deployable rectangular solar panels on opposite sides, camera/instrument on the nadir face, small antennas.

draw-micro-labsat.description: ~54 kg box microsat (about 60 x 60 x 50 cm) with body-mounted solar cells, small cameras, flew piggyback on H-IIA F4.

draw-servis.description: ~980 kg MELCO-built box bus with two deployable solar wings, test-component trays on the body; SERVIS-1 and -2 are the same design.

draw-socrates.description: A 50 cm cube with every face covered in dark blue solar cells (no solar wings at all). On one face a small round laser-terminal telescope sits on a two-axis gimbal. A couple of short antennas. Earth's limb below has blue oceans and white clouds (not orange).

draw-sohla-1.description: Spin-stabilised 50 cm cube, 50 kg, solar cells on the faces, short antennas; built by Higashi-Osaka SMEs with JAXA support.

draw-sstl-microsat-70.description: ~50-70 kg SSTL box (about 60 x 35 x 35 cm stack of module trays) with body-mounted solar panels on four sides and a short gravity-gradient boom / whip antennas.

draw-cast968.description: ~350-470 kg box with two deployable solar wings; HJ-1A/B carry wide-field cameras on the nadir face (HJ-1A adds a hyperspectral imager).

draw-lilacsat-2.description: 11 kg cube 20 x 20 x 20 cm, body-mounted solar cells, VHF/UHF whip antennas; Harbin Institute of Technology amateur/edu sat.

draw-yaogan-1-sar.description: A large rectangular box-shaped spacecraft bus with a very long, flat, rectangular radar antenna panel (dark, gridded, about three times the body's length and as tall as the body) mounted lengthwise along one side, plus two rectangular solar wings on the other sides. Earth's limb below has blue oceans and white clouds (not orange).

draw-wn5000.description: ~40-70 kg box microsat with two deployable fixed solar panels; Spark 01/02 hyperspectral imagers and Yijian share it.

draw-zhuhai-1-ohs.description: ~67 kg box microsat, two deployable solar panels, hyperspectral camera on the nadir face (Orbita Aerospace, 2018-2019 batches).

draw-phoenix-eye-2.description: A large box-shaped bus with two rectangular solar wings. On its Earth-facing underside three camera barrels point down at different angles, one forward, one straight down, one backward, plus a fourth smaller camera. Earth's limb below has blue oceans and white clouds (not orange).

draw-leostar-500-xo.description: ~750-900 kg hexagonal bus about 2.1 m tall and 2 m wide, one deployable fixed solar array, large Earth-pointing telescope. Earth's limb below has blue oceans and white clouds (not orange).

draw-astrosat-100.description: ~120 kg cube about 60 cm, four small deployable solar panels in a cross/fan, Korsch telescope (NAOMI) on one face.
